cards.explanation: The answer is a man's envy of his neighbor. The Teacher, the writer of Ecclesiastes, says all labor and success spring “…from a man’s envy of his neighbor.” Not love, not hunger, just a long look over the fence. He calls it “…a pursuit of the wind.” and I think that means you can sprint all day and still catch nothing.

The answer is the fool, friends. The Teacher says, “The fool folds his hands and consumes his own flesh.” I'm picturing somebody leaning back with those folded hands. It's a sharp little line, and it sits right next to all that envy-driven labor, so the Teacher has both sides of the picture covered.

The better one is one handful with tranquility, friends. The Teacher says, “Better one handful with tranquility than two handfuls with toil and pursuit of the wind.” Less, but with calm, beats more, but with a fight. I'd put that on a cookie box if the lid were bigger.

The answer is True. The Teacher says that though this man's labor has no end, “…his eyes are still not content with his wealth…” He has the wealth, and his eyes still aren't content with it. That's the part that makes it hard to watch.

The man wants to know who he is working so hard for. He asks, “For whom do I toil and bereave my soul of enjoyment?” He's all alone, with no son or brother, and he stops to ask who all this work is for. I think that's a question worth asking before the work piles up.

The word is miserable, bakers. The Teacher says, “This too is futile—a miserable task.” It's about a man alone, working without end, asking, “For whom do I toil and bereave my soul of enjoyment?” I think that's about as heavy as this passage gets, so I'll just say it plainly and move on.

The answer is that two have a good return for their labor. The Teacher says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor.” Just before this, a lonely man asks, “For whom do I toil…” and this is the turn. Two people have a good return for their labor.

His companion can lift him up, friends. The Teacher says, “For if one falls down, his companion can lift him up…” That's the whole point of having a companion. You don't have to dust yourself off alone.

The answer is True. The Teacher says, “Again, if two lie down together, they will keep warm; but how can one keep warm alone?” I think he asks it because the answer is already sitting there. My ovens keep the bakery toasty, but I'd still take company over a warm oven.
The word is overpowered, friends. The Teacher says, “And though one may be overpowered, two can resist.” One person alone can lose a struggle. Two standing together can hold their ground.

The answer is False. The Teacher says, “Moreover, a cord of three strands is not quickly broken.” He started with one, moved to two, and then adds a third strand. It's the strongest picture of the bunch.

A poor but wise youth is the better one, friends. The Teacher says, “Better is a poor but wise youth than an old but foolish king who no longer knows how to take a warning.” Wisdom beats the crown here. And notice what the text says about the king: he no longer knows how to take a warning.

All the living followed him, friends. The Teacher says, “I saw that all who lived and walked under the sun followed this second one, the youth who succeeded the king.” That's a huge crowd behind one person. The Teacher doesn't say why they followed.

The answer is False. The Teacher says, “Yet the successor will not be celebrated by those who come even later.” Even a youth who came from the prison to the kingship (Ecclesiastes 4:14) isn't celebrated by those who come even later. And then the Teacher says it again: “This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind.”
